s1: SAKSI. Witness validated secret sharing, over the Mersenne prime field, two to the power one hundred and twenty seven, minus one. An entry for the cryptographic track.
s2: A master key kept in one place is one leak away from disaster. Shamir secret sharing fixes that, but it has a quiet flaw. It never checks the shares. One lying custodian can hand in a fake share, and everyone else rebuilds the wrong key without knowing. Tompa and Woll showed this in 1988.
s3: SAKSI encodes the key as field elements, and multiplies them by a Vandermonde matrix to make n shares. Any t shares rebuild the key. Any t minus one learn nothing at all: that is perfect secrecy. Every share then gets one time witness tags. Each tag is an affine function of the share, its index, its session and its epoch, keyed by another custodian. Reconstruction runs in two rounds: shares and tags first, keys second. A share needs a majority of witnesses to confirm it. The accepted shares must also pass a Reed Solomon syndrome check, before Lagrange interpolation releases the key. There is no block cipher, no hash, and no pre existing encryption algorithm anywhere in the key path.
s4: Here is the Rust core, running in the browser as WebAssembly. I split a credential across five custodians, with a threshold of three. Now custodian two forges its share, and custodian four lies with false keys. Run the reveal. Share two gets zero confirmations out of four. Both liars are named, and the key is still correct. Plain Shamir, given the same shares, silently returns a wrong key.
s5: This is the applicable environment. An AI agent answers questions about a small Malaysian business's ledger. When it needs the API credential, SAKSI rebuilds it inside the browser for about a millisecond, makes one request, and drops it. The language model only ever sees the result. Every request to the model is scanned for fragments of the credential, and none are found. If three of the five custodians lie, the agent is refused: SAKSI fails closed.
s6: Does it survive cryptanalysis? I attacked it myself. Exhaustive enumeration in small fields shows that zero bits leak below the threshold. A Z3 solver extracts seven bits from a Mignotte control, and nothing from SAKSI. Measured forgery rates match one over p. Across eight active attacks, including Tompa Woll, replay, cross session substitution and colluding liars, plain Shamir was fooled up to one hundred percent of the time. SAKSI returned a wrong key zero times, and named every cheater. Two thousand fuzzed inputs caused zero crashes.
s7: To minimise the attack surface against side channels, the core is written in Rust with branch free arithmetic: Mersenne reduction, fixed shape multiplication, a fixed length inversion ladder, and constant time comparison. A dudect timing test with one million samples finds no leak in any operation, while two deliberately leaky controls are caught immediately.
s8: Everything is written up in a thirteen page LaTeX paper, with proofs of perfect secrecy, a one over p forgery bound, and robustness against up to half the custodians lying. It is candid about the limits: a trusted dealer per epoch, key material that grows with n squared, and the need for an honest majority. With three of five colluding, the bound is tight, and the paper shows that too.
s9: SAKSI. In Malay, saksi means witness. The code, the paper and the live demo are linked below.
